newsitem.title: USA: Challenger sees US wage pressures starting to rise.
newsitem.headline: Challenger sees US wage pressures starting to rise.

text.p: With the labor market continuing to tighten, wage pressures should start to become more visible, said a top executive of a U.S. outplacement firm.
John Challenger, executive vice president of Challenger, Gray & Christmas, said that "wage pressures are building," although the "flood gates won't open."

A confluence of factors, from a drop in the unemployment rate to 4.9 percent, a fall in temporary jobs and a decline in the percentage of entrepeneurs suggests that "we may be nearing ... full employment," Challenger said.

"We are seeing a lot of factors we haven't seen before come together," Challenger said in an intervioew with Reuters. "People are saying 'Why take a temporary job? Why start a business? Why not take advantage of what is out there?'
But not everyone is reaping the benefits of the healthy labor market.
Despite workers finally having the upper hand, the big wage gains are being seen only for top performing employees -- which account for about 25 percent of the workforce, Challenger said.
To offset wage gains firms are lowering base pay for the other 75 percent, Challenger said, and giving bonuses for good performance.
Large gains also are being seen by independent consultants.
He noted that industries where workers can receieve higher wages are mostly technological- and computer-related. And, he said, the markets were waiting for college graduates with computer experience.
As hiring continues layoffs also are contuniung at a rapid pace, Challenger said, but most of those who are laid off find jobs.

Challenger predicted that the utility sector will be next to lay off workers in large numbers. He said that most other large industries (such as airlines and telecommunications) have gone through deregulation.
"Electric, gas and power have yet to go through it in the same way. It seems they are on the brink of changes. "But it's going to be tough, some skills aren't directly transferable" to other sectors.
Challenger said that the work force in the 1990s has been through a watershed. Companies are not keeping excessive workers, rather firms have reverted to "just in time hiring,": he said.
Meanwhile, many older workers have returned to their former companies in part-time roles, which he said benefits the companies because they get expertise without having to hire full-time workers.
